title: Van Kampen diagrams
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: Van Kampen diagrams developed combinatorially, without the Jordan curve theorem. The first lesson defines plane maps as sphere maps with an outer face and proves the facts used about them: faces and Euler's formula, deleting an edge between two faces or with one face, contracting an edge, pendant edges, chords, loops in a corner, and cutting along a loop. The second treats words and free reduction with the normal form, the free group, groups given by generators and relators, walks up to backtracking with the fundamental group of a graph and closed walks in trees, and Cayley graphs with label-preserving maps. The third proves van Kampen's lemma in three parts: a word that is a product of k conjugates of relators has a diagram with at most k bounded faces; the exterior walk of a diagram is homotopic to a product of conjugates of its face walks, one for each bounded face; and every closed walk of a diagram has a label representing the identity, so that the diagram maps to the Cayley graph. These are the statements (VK) and (MAP) used by the courses on irrational traces, the Kadison-Kaplansky conjecture and reduced Baum-Connes injectivity.
prerequisites: programme course Barnette's conjecture (barnettes-conjecture): lesson Sphere maps (Definition 1.1, Lemma 1.2, Example 1.3, Lemma 1.4, Lemma 1.5, Proposition 1.6, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Lemma 3.4, Proposition 3.5, Section 4 and Proposition 4.1)

checks.reading: Classical material, written independently on the combinatorial framework of the lesson Sphere maps of barnettes-conjecture. Compared on 16 Oct 2026: Bridson, The geometry of the word problem (author's page; introduction and contents, Section 1 with Definition 1.2.2, Section 4 with Definitions 4.1.1 and 4.2.1, Proposition 4.1.2, Theorem 4.2.2 and Lemmas 4.2.3 and 4.2.6, where diagrams are singular discs in the plane); Erickson, Computational Topology (author's page; Sections 9.4, 9.5, 9.8, 10.2, 10.4 and 10.6). Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (author's page), Sections 1.2, 1.3 and 1.A, is cited as further reading. Changes of form against Bridson's treatment: plane graphs are plane maps (sphere maps with an outer face), so every statement is combinatorial; the reduction of a cancelling pair on the boundary (Bridson's Lemma 4.2.3, an arc and a collapse in the plane) becomes a chord, a contraction and a deletion, or a chord and a cut along a loop; the base of a diagram is a dart of the outer face. E. R. van Kampen is named for credit only. Check program plan/checks_20261016/vk_check.py (output vk_check_run_20261016a.txt, 16 Oct 2026): 16,278 checks, 0 failures. 300 random plane maps built from pendant edges and chords: every deletion of an edge between two faces merges them as stated, every bridge leaves two sphere maps, every contraction of a non-loop keeps the faces with the edge removed; 1,500 random presentations with up to three relators of length up to five and products of up to four conjugates: the bouquet of Lemma 2.1 built step by step has the product as exterior word and one bounded face per factor (and agrees with an explicit construction), the cancellations of Lemma 2.3 (all cases: 662 spikes, 3,143 contractions, 154 cuts along a loop, 40 whole-walk cancellations, including 169 with degenerate corners) and the insertions of Lemma 2.2 give a diagram whose exterior word is exactly the given word, with at most as many bounded faces as factors, all with relator labels; the product of conjugates of Theorem 4.1 is homotopic to the exterior walk in every case; for 300 diagrams over a presentation of the symmetric group S_3 the label-preserving map of Theorem 5.1 exists.
